title: Organic nitrogen: amines, basicity and diazonium chemistry
subject: Chemistry

chapters.title: Count the carbon groups bonded to nitrogen
chapters.formula: Primary RNH2; secondary R2NH; tertiary R3N; quaternary R4N+
chapters.script: Welcome to Organic Nitrogen. This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice. Classify an amine by counting carbon groups directly bonded to nitrogen. One carbon group gives a primary amine, two give a secondary amine and three give a tertiary amine. Branching elsewhere in the carbon skeleton does not change that count. Thus tert butylamine is primary even though the carbon attached to nitrogen has three carbon neighbours. Dimethylamine is secondary and trimethylamine is tertiary. A quaternary ammonium ion has four carbon groups on nitrogen and a positive charge; it is a different class from a neutral tertiary amine. In aniline, nitrogen is directly attached to a benzene ring, allowing its lone pair to conjugate with the ring. In benzylamine, a saturated carbon separates nitrogen from the ring. That difference affects basicity and reactivity. An amide instead has nitrogen directly attached to a carbonyl carbon. Delocalization into the carbonyl strongly reduces the nitrogen lone pair's availability compared with an ordinary amine. Draw nitrogen's immediate neighbours before classifying a structure.
points: Primary · 1 · tert-Butylamine
Secondary · 2 · Dimethylamine
Tertiary · 3 · Trimethylamine

chapters.title: The lone pair accepts a proton
chapters.formula: pKₐ = −log₁₀ Kₐ; pKᵦ = −log₁₀ Kᵦ; pKₐ + pKᵦ = 14 at 25°C
chapters.script: An amine's nitrogen lone pair can accept a proton to form an ammonium ion. Basicity measures the equilibrium tendency for that proton transfer in a specified solvent. A larger base equilibrium constant means a stronger base under comparable conditions. The conjugate acid and base constants are related through the water ion product. At twenty five degrees Celsius, take that product as ten raised to the power minus fourteen. If the conjugate acid has an acid constant of ten to the minus ten, dividing the water ion product by it gives a base constant of ten to the minus four. The corresponding acid and base logarithmic values are ten and four, adding to fourteen. An acid logarithmic value of five instead gives a base logarithmic value of nine, indicating a weaker base. Always identify whether the supplied value describes the amine or its conjugate acid. Structural effects help explain the comparison: alkyl groups can donate electron density, while aniline's nitrogen lone pair participates in aromatic conjugation. Electron withdrawing substituents, steric crowding and solvent stabilization can all affect the observed equilibrium.
points: 10 · 4 · Stronger base
5 · 9 · Weaker base
Same solvent · pKₐ + pKᵦ = 14 · Illustrative values

chapters.title: Do not use a gas-phase ranking blindly in water
chapters.formula: At the same temperature for a conjugate pair: K_a K_b = K_w
chapters.script: Alkyl groups can donate electron density, suggesting increased intrinsic proton affinity as substitution increases. In water, however, the neutral amine and its conjugate acid are solvated differently. Hydrogen bonding, steric crowding and solvation of the charged product can change the ordering. A universal tertiary > secondary > primary rule in aqueous solution is unreliable. If a problem supplies K b or conjugate-acid p K a values measured under comparable conditions, use those data rather than a memorized slogan. For example, a conjugate acid with p K a 10 corresponds to a stronger base than one with p K a 5 in the same solvent and convention. These numbers are illustrative, not values assigned to unspecified real compounds. For illustrative bases A and B with conjugate acid p K a values ten and five, their acid constants differ by one hundred thousand. Their base constants differ by the inverse factor, making A the stronger base by that equilibrium measure. This is a ratio of constants under comparable conditions, not a statement that every solution has a one hundred thousand fold difference in p H or reaction rate.
points: Alkyl donation · Electron availability · Intrinsic tendency

chapters.title: Preparation can keep or reduce the carbon count
chapters.formula: R-C#N -> R-CH2NH2; R-CONH2 -> R-NH2 in Hofmann rearrangement
chapters.script: Preparation of an amine must be checked by following every carbon atom. A nitrile contains a carbon bonded to nitrogen through a triple bond. Suitable reduction converts that nitrile carbon into the carbon of a methylene group attached to amino nitrogen. Acetonitrile starts with two carbons and gives ethylamine, which still has two. Reduction of an aromatic nitro group can give aniline without changing the ring's carbon framework. A different preparation, Hofmann rearrangement of a primary amide, shortens the carbon chain of the organic amine by one. Acetamide has two carbons but gives methylamine with one carbon because its carbonyl carbon leaves the selected organic product. That carbon remains accounted for elsewhere in the overall reaction. Ammonia reacting with a suitable alkyl halide can form an amine, but further alkylation may produce mixtures. Gabriel synthesis is another route for suitable primary alkyl substrates and does not imply ordinary substitution on an unactivated aryl halide. Identify the starting functional group, select appropriate conditions and compare the carbon counts before naming the final amine.

chapters.title: Identification depends on the nitrogen class
chapters.formula: Test interpretation: identify whether nitrogen originally carries one or two N-H bonds
chapters.script: The carbylamine test is associated with primary aliphatic and aromatic amines; secondary and tertiary amines do not give that same reaction. It produces an isocyanide under the specified test conditions.  In the Hinsberg distinction, primary and secondary amines can form different sulfonamide products, while tertiary amines do not form the same nitrogen hydrogen-derived product. A primary-amine sulfonamide retains an acidic nitrogen hydrogen and can dissolve in alkali; the secondary-amine product lacks that hydrogen and is not similarly alkali-soluble. Check the subsequent acid/base behaviour rather than relying only on a precipitate. The primary amine starting material has two nitrogen hydrogen bonds; its sulfonamide product retains one. A secondary amine begins with one such hydrogen and loses it during sulfonamide formation, leaving no nitrogen hydrogen in that product. This explains the different alkaline behaviour more precisely than saying primary amines dissolve and secondary amines never dissolve. Solubility also depends on protonation, solvent and the exact compound.
points: Primary · Retains acidic N–H · Can dissolve
Secondary · No remaining N–H · Not similarly soluble
Tertiary · No same sulfonamide · Check acid response

chapters.title: Nitrous acid distinguishes aromatic diazotization
chapters.formula: Ar-NH2 --nitrous acid, cold acidic solution--> Ar-N2+
chapters.script: Aniline reacts with nitrous acid generated under cold acidic conditions to form a benzenediazonium salt. The usual elementary temperature window is about two hundred seventy three to two hundred seventy eight kelvin. Aromatic diazonium salts are useful intermediates in cold solution; they should not be described as indefinitely stable or safe to isolate dry. A primary aliphatic amine can form a much less stable aliphatic diazonium species that loses nitrogen and leads to further products. Secondary amines instead can form N-nitrosamines under appropriate nitrosating conditions; they do not follow the same primary aromatic diazotization sequence. Always identify the original nitrogen class and the aromatic attachment before choosing the pathway. Cold aromatic diazonium formation and later warming are separate stages with different purposes. In a conceptual aniline to phenol sequence, first create the diazonium group under suitable cold acidic conditions, then replace it during aqueous warming. The six ring carbons remain throughout. Different classes of amines react differently with nitrous acid, so the reagent name alone cannot establish that a diazonium salt is the final product.
points: Primary aromatic · Diazonium formation · Cold acidic solution
Primary aliphatic · Unstable intermediate · Further products
Secondary · Nitrosamine possible · Different pathway

chapters.title: A diazonium group can be replaced
chapters.formula: Ar-N2+ -> Ar-OH + N2 under suitable aqueous warming conditions
chapters.script: A benzenediazonium group can be replaced by chloride or bromide using suitable copper halide with copper in oxidation state plus one conditions, or by cyanide using the corresponding copper reagent in a Sandmeyer transformation. Iodide substitution and other replacement routes use different conditions. Write the reagent explicitly instead of treating every replacement as the same copper-catalysed process. Warming a suitable aqueous diazonium solution can give phenol with nitrogen loss. Introducing CN adds a carbon to the organic product; replacing the group with hydroxyl or Cl does not. Diazonium chemistry therefore connects amines with aromatic compounds that are difficult to obtain by simple direct substitution of an ordinary aryl halide. Replacing the diazonium group of a six carbon ring by chlorine preserves six carbons. Replacing it by a cyano group gives a seven carbon nitrile because the new group contains carbon. Nitrogen gas loss occurs in either replacement, yet the final organic nitrogen content differs: the cyano product still contains a nitrogen atom from the introduced reagent. Track each group's source rather than counting only the starting nitrogen.
points: Chloride · Cl · 6 + 0 = 6
Cyanide · CN · 6 + 1 = 7
Aqueous warming · OH · 6 + 0 = 6

board.heading: A diazonium group can be replaced

chapters.title: Coupling makes a bond to another aromatic ring
chapters.formula: Azo coupling retains nitrogen: Ar-N=N-Ar'; diazonium replacement commonly releases N2
chapters.script: A diazonium species can act as an electrophile towards an activated aromatic ring, producing an azo linkage joining two aromatic groups. Phenol is commonly coupled under suitably alkaline conditions and aniline under controlled mildly acidic conditions. The medium matters because it controls ring activation and the form of the reacting groups. Coupling often favours the para site when it is available; an occupied para position can change the outcome. Conjugated azo products can be strongly coloured, but not every colour or shade is predictable from a reaction label alone. For synthesis questions, track whether nitrogen is retained as an azo bridge or lost as nitrogen gas during replacement. Azo coupling joins two aromatic partners through a nitrogen nitrogen double bond. If each partner is a six carbon ring without carbon side chains, the product contains twelve carbons and the azo bridge contributes no carbon. Replacement of a diazonium group by hydroxyl instead keeps only the original ring in that product. These different outcomes explain why coupling and replacement cannot be treated as interchangeable arrows in a synthesis plan.
points: Azo coupling · Retained in –N=N– · 6 + 6 = 12
OH replacement · N₂ released · 6 C ring retained
Coupling site · Often para if free · Medium matters

chapters.title: Choose amine routes by carbon count
chapters.formula: Nitrile reduction retains C; Hofmann amide rearrangement loses one C
chapters.script: Amine preparation routes can give different carbon skeletons even when all products are primary amines. Reduction of propanenitrile retains its nitrile carbon, producing the three carbon primary amine propylamine. In contrast, Hofmann rearrangement of propanamide produces ethylamine, with one fewer carbon than the starting amide. The amide carbonyl carbon does not remain in that amine skeleton. Gabriel synthesis provides another planning route: a suitable primary alkyl halide is converted through a phthalimide intermediate and then released as a primary amine. Bromoethane can therefore lead to ethylamine without adding a carbon to its ethyl group. Ordinary Gabriel alkylation is not a general preparation of aniline from an aryl halide, because the required substitution chemistry is different. Do not confuse the names Hofmann rearrangement and Hofmann elimination; they describe different transformations. Write the carbon count beside both starting material and proposed product before choosing a named reaction. The route must fit the substrate as well as the desired nitrogen substitution class.
points: Propanenitrile reduction · Retain nitrile carbon · Propylamine; 3 C
Propanamide rearrangement · Lose carbonyl carbon · Ethylamine; 2 C
Gabriel: ethyl halide · Suitable alkyl substitution · Ethylamine; 2 C

chapters.title: Amine acylation and protection
chapters.formula: Primary / secondary amines form amides; ordinary tertiary amines lack N–H
chapters.script: Acylation attaches an acyl group to a nitrogen nucleophile and changes its electronic properties. A primary or secondary amine with a nitrogen hydrogen can form an amide with a suitable acylating reagent. A tertiary amine has no nitrogen hydrogen and does not give the same ordinary neutral amide by this substitution. It may still participate in other reactions or act as a base, so the absence of that product is not universal inertness. Aniline can be converted into acetanilide by introducing an acetyl group on nitrogen. The nitrogen lone pair then interacts with the carbonyl, reducing its availability and moderating the strong activation associated with free amino substitution on the ring. This is useful in reaction planning where the amino group must be protected or its reactivity controlled. Subsequent suitable hydrolysis can restore the amine. Acylation is distinct from alkylation: the new group contains a carbonyl and the product is an amide. Track the atom receiving the group instead of assuming every new carbon group on nitrogen produces another simple amine.
points: Primary / secondary amine · N–H available · Amide formation possible
Tertiary amine · No N–H · Not the same neutral amide
Aniline acylation · Acetyl group on N · Acetanilide; moderated reactivity

chapters.title: Interpret Hinsberg observations
chapters.formula: Sulfonamide N–H controls the introductory alkali-solubility distinction
chapters.script: The Hinsberg comparison distinguishes amine classes through reaction and solubility evidence rather than by counting alkyl groups in a name alone. In the standard model, a primary amine forms a sulfonamide that retains a nitrogen hydrogen. That hydrogen can be removed by alkali, giving a soluble ionic form under the stated conditions. Acidification can return the neutral sulfonamide. A secondary amine forms a sulfonamide without that nitrogen hydrogen, so it lacks the same alkali dissolution step in the introductory comparison. A tertiary amine does not form the corresponding sulfonamide in this test but can dissolve in dilute acid by forming an ammonium salt. Distinguish absence of a derivative from inability to form any salt. The observations depend on the specified substrate and medium, and solubility on its own is not a complete structure identification. Draw the nitrogen substituents in the proposed derivative before selecting the class. This reasoning concerns interpretation of a supplied test sequence, not a procedure for handling the reagent in a laboratory.
points: Primary amine derivative · Sulfonamide N–H remains · Can dissolve in alkali
Secondary amine derivative · No sulfonamide N–H · No same dissolution step
Tertiary amine · No corresponding derivative · Can form acid-soluble salt

chapters.title: Diazonium replacements and carbon ledgers
chapters.formula: Ring–N₂⁺ can be replaced; incoming CN adds one carbon
chapters.script: An aromatic diazonium group is a useful junction for several replacement reactions. In the usual aniline preparation, nitrous acid is generated under cold acidic conditions and the diazonium salt is handled as a condition dependent intermediate. Different reagents then lead to different ring substituents. Copper one chloride or bromide supports the corresponding halogen replacement in the familiar Sandmeyer pattern. Copper one cyanide introduces a nitrile group, while suitable warm aqueous conditions can lead to phenol with nitrogen release. Count carbons when the incoming group contains carbon. Starting from a six carbon aniline ring, replacement by hydroxyl gives a six carbon phenol, but replacement by cyanide gives seven carbon benzonitrile. Hydrolysis of that nitrile can then give seven carbon benzoic acid. The nitrogen atoms in the departing diazonium group do not become the nitrile nitrogen by simple retention; identify the incoming reagent. Reaction maps should label both the replacing group and the conditions, rather than drawing one unspecified arrow that could mean several incompatible products.
points: Ring–N₂⁺ → ring–OH · Suitable aqueous conversion · Phenol; 6 C

chapters.title: Quantify base strength with pKb
chapters.formula: At 25 °C in water: pKa(BH⁺) + pKb(B) ≈ 14
chapters.script: Base strength comparisons become quantitative when the constants refer to the same solvent and temperature. A smaller p K b means a larger base dissociation constant. For illustrative bases with p K b values four and nine in water at twenty five degrees Celsius, their base constants are ten to the minus four and ten to the minus nine. The first is one hundred thousand times larger. This ratio does not mean the hydroxide concentrations must have the same ratio in arbitrary solutions, because concentration and equilibrium balances still matter. For a conjugate acid and base pair in water, their constants multiply to the water ion product. At this temperature, p K a of the conjugate acid plus p K b of the base is approximately fourteen. Thus a base with p K b four has conjugate acid p K a about ten. At a different temperature, use the appropriate water constant. Do not combine a gas phase basicity ranking with aqueous constants or assume that electron donation, resonance and solvation always produce the same amine ordering.

chapters.title: Gabriel synthesis has a substrate boundary
chapters.formula: Suitable primary alkyl halide → primary alkylamine; not an ordinary aryl substitution
chapters.script: The Gabriel synthesis is a reaction planning tool for a suitable primary alkylamine, rather than a promise that every halide gives any desired amine. In the elementary scheme, a phthalimide nitrogen nucleophile displaces halide from a suitable alkyl carbon. Subsequent cleavage of the protecting imide framework releases the primary amine. With a two carbon alkyl fragment, the resulting amine contains that same two carbon fragment attached to nitrogen. The imide ring is a temporary carrier; its carbons are not all incorporated into the target alkylamine. Ordinary unactivated chlorobenzene does not undergo the same backside displacement at its aromatic carbon, so this simple route is not a general preparation of aniline from chlorobenzene. Tertiary alkyl substrates also do not become good ordinary backside substitution partners merely because the named reaction is requested. The method avoids describing an uncontrolled sequence of repeated alkylations as a selective preparation of one primary amine. Identify the reacting carbon, its substitution pattern, and the nitrogen containing fragment that remains after release. These are connectivity predictions for the stated model, not experimental handling instructions or a claim that every substrate gives quantitative conversion.

chapters.title: Nitrous-acid gas data need the amine class
chapters.formula: Ideal primary aliphatic amine model: 1 mol amine → 1 mol N₂
chapters.script: Gas evolution from a nitrogen reaction must be interpreted with the substrate class and the gas collection model stated. A simple primary aliphatic amine can react through an unstable aliphatic diazonium intermediate that loses nitrogen gas. In the elementary quantitative model, each mole of reacting primary amine gives one mole of nitrogen molecules, although the organic product distribution need not be uniquely predicted for every substrate. Suppose a supplied experiment reports twenty four point zero millilitres of dry nitrogen at three hundred kelvin and one hundred kilopascals, with ideal gas behaviour and quantitative collection. Use R equal to eight point three one four litre kilopascals per mole kelvin. The nitrogen amount is about zero point zero zero zero nine six two mole. That is also the reacting amine amount under the one to one model. A twenty five point zero millilitre aliquot would therefore contain about zero point zero three eight five molar reactive primary amine. Wet gas would need a water vapour correction. A primary aromatic amine can instead form an arenediazonium salt under the specified diazotization conditions; do not automatically apply the same immediate gas assay to every nitrogen compound.

chapters.title: An amide nitrogen is not a simple alkylamine nitrogen
chapters.formula: Carbonyl delocalization reduces availability of the amide nitrogen lone pair
chapters.script: The presence of a nitrogen atom does not make every nitrogen compound equally basic. In a simple alkylamine, the nitrogen lone pair can accept a proton, with measured basicity also depending on solvent and other structural effects. In an amide, that lone pair interacts with the adjacent carbonyl system. Resonance descriptions include a contribution with positive charge on nitrogen and negative charge on oxygen, while the real molecule is not switching between isolated drawings. The carbon nitrogen bond consequently has partial double bond character, and the nitrogen lone pair is less freely available than in the corresponding simple amine. Under ordinary strongly acidic protonation discussions, amides commonly protonate preferentially on oxygen rather than behaving exactly like an alkylamine at nitrogen. This explains why converting an amine into an amide changes its basicity and is useful in protection strategies. It does not mean every amide is completely unable to interact with acid or that a resonance drawing supplies a numerical base constant. Compare actual structures and matching solvent data. An amine classification based on carbon groups directly bonded to nitrogen also should not silently replace the distinct functional group identification of an amide.

chapters.title: Track both nitrogens in diazonium reactions
chapters.formula: Diazonium replacement loses N₂; azo coupling retains the N–N unit
chapters.script: A nitrogen atom ledger distinguishes diazonium replacement from azo coupling. In the elementary diazotization accounting, one nitrogen comes from the original primary aromatic amino group and another from the nitrosating source. The arenediazonium group therefore contains two nitrogen atoms attached as a single group to the aromatic framework. In a replacement reaction that releases nitrogen gas, both atoms leave that organic framework together as one nitrogen molecule. The incoming replacement group can have its own atoms, so product composition must still be counted separately. In azo coupling with an appropriate activated aromatic partner, the nitrogen nitrogen unit is retained between the two aromatic fragments instead. A benzene derived diazonium fragment has six carbons; a phenol partner contributes another six. The simple hydroxyazobenzene connectivity contains twelve carbons and two azo nitrogens. If an isotope marks one of the nitrogen sources in the ideal accounting model, replacement sends that marked atom into the released nitrogen, while coupling retains it in the azo unit. This ledger does not specify every isotope exchange pathway, the coupling position under every condition, or an experimental isolation procedure. Use it to distinguish which bond connection and which atom inventory are actually being tested.

chapters.title: Carbylamine equation and the extra carbon
chapters.formula: RNH₂ + CHCl₃ + 3KOH → RNC + 3KCl + 3H₂O
chapters.script: The carbylamine reaction is useful as a structural identification principle for primary amines. In its familiar net equation, one primary amine combines with one chloroform and three potassium hydroxide units to form an isocyanide, three potassium chloride units and three water molecules. Both primary aliphatic and primary aromatic amines can fit this standard test. Ordinary secondary and tertiary amines do not give the corresponding positive test. The product connectivity matters: an isocyanide has the organic group bonded to nitrogen, followed by the terminal carbon. A nitrile instead has the organic group bonded directly to the nitrile carbon. Starting with ethylamine, the two carbon ethyl group remains attached to nitrogen, while chloroform supplies a third carbon to the isocyanide group. This does not extend the ethyl carbon chain into a propyl group. In a stipulated complete net conversion of zero point zero one zero zero mole primary amine, the theoretical isocyanide amount is the same and the hydroxide amount is three times as large. This equation is an atom ledger and identification concept, not an instruction to perform or smell a hazardous test.

chapters.title: Successive methylation ends in an ammonium salt
chapters.formula: CH₃NH₂ → (CH₃)₂NH → (CH₃)₃N → [(CH₃)₄N]⁺
chapters.script: An amine alkylation question must distinguish a desired substitution from further reaction of the product. Consider a stipulated sequence of successive methylations beginning with methylamine. The first added methyl group gives dimethylamine, and a second gives trimethylamine. These steps replace nitrogen hydrogen bonds with nitrogen carbon bonds after the necessary proton transfer. A third added methyl group gives tetramethylammonium, which can be present as its iodide salt when methyl iodide supplies the groups. Count the carbons: the starting amine contains one methyl carbon and the final cation contains four. Count nitrogen bonds separately. Trimethylamine has three carbon bonds and a lone pair, whereas the quaternary ammonium ion has four carbon bonds and a positive formal charge. It is not normally classified as a fourth degree amine with an available lone pair for ordinary amine protonation. In actual alkylation, product mixtures and repeated alkylation can make selective preparation difficult. The arrow sequence therefore describes possible successive transformations, not a promise that each reagent addition yields one pure intermediate. Track added groups, nitrogen hydrogen bonds and charge at every stage.

chapters.title: Known pH fixes the protonated amine fraction
chapters.formula: [BH⁺]/[B] = 10^(pKaH − pH); neutral fraction = 1/(1 + ratio)
chapters.script: The basicity of an amine also determines how much is neutral at a specified solution pH. Write the conjugate acid equilibrium as protonated base giving neutral base and a proton. In the ideal concentration approximation, the ratio of protonated to neutral base equals ten raised to the conjugate acid p K a minus the p H. Suppose the supplied conjugate acid p K a is nine and an external system maintains p H seven. The ratio is one hundred to one, so the neutral fraction is one divided by one hundred and one, approximately zero point nine nine percent. The protonated fraction is approximately ninety nine point zero one percent. At maintained p H eleven the ratio reverses to one to one hundred, and the neutral fraction becomes approximately ninety nine point zero one percent. These calculations use the stated p H; they do not determine the p H of an isolated weak base solution from its analytical concentration. Acidic aqueous conditions can therefore favour an ammonium salt, while increased p H can increase the neutral amine fraction. Partition into another phase would need additional equilibrium information.

chapters.title: Protection changes aniline bromination selectivity
chapters.formula: Aniline → acetanilide → mainly para-bromoacetanilide → para-bromoaniline
chapters.script: The amino group strongly activates an aromatic ring toward electrophilic substitution. In the familiar bromine water comparison, aniline can give two four six tribromoaniline rather than stopping at one bromine substituent. A protection strategy changes that behaviour. Acylating the amino group gives acetanilide, whose nitrogen lone pair is also involved with the carbonyl group. Under suitable controlled bromination conditions, the protected ring gives mainly the para brominated product. Hydrolysis of the protecting group then gives para bromoaniline. The para preference is a usual major product description, not a universal claim of complete selectivity under every condition. Follow the temporary carbon inventory as well as the bromine count. Aniline begins with six carbons, acetyl protection adds two, and bromination leaves all eight carbons in the protected molecule. Removal of the acetyl group returns the target amine to six carbons. Direct tribromination installs three bromines, whereas the protected monobromination route targets one. A protecting group therefore changes reactivity temporarily and is later removed; it is not an extra carbon fragment retained in the intended final aromatic amine.

chapters.title: Nitro reduction has a six-electron nitrogen ledger
chapters.formula: ArNO₂ + 6H⁺ + 6e⁻ → ArNH₂ + 2H₂O; add H⁺ for ArNH₃⁺
chapters.script: Reducing a nitro group to an amine retains the nitrogen and carbon skeleton but changes the nitrogen oxidation state. For a nitro group bonded to carbon, nitrogen is formally plus three; in the corresponding primary amine it is minus three. The change therefore requires six electrons per nitrogen. A balanced acidic half reaction can be written with one nitro compound, six hydrogen ions and six electrons forming the neutral amine and two waters. If the specified product is the protonated amine in an acidic mixture, add one more hydrogen ion and write an ammonium product instead. That extra proton is acid base bookkeeping, not a seventh reduction electron. Thus an ideal zero point zero one zero zero mole nitrobenzene conversion needs zero point zero six zero zero mole electrons for aniline formation. Actual reagent demand also depends on competing reactions and the oxidation product of the reducing agent. Do not replace the nitro nitrogen with nitrogen from the acid or assume that it leaves as nitrogen gas. This reduction is different from diazonium replacement and from an amide rearrangement that changes carbon count.

Neutral amine half reaction · 6H⁺ + 6e⁻; two waters · Atoms and charge balanced

chapters.title: Supporting distinction: Hofmann elimination is not rearrangement
chapters.formula: [CH₃CH₂N(CH₃)₃]⁺ OH⁻ → CH₂=CH₂ + N(CH₃)₃ + H₂O
chapters.script: Two reactions named Hofmann must not be confused. The amide rearrangement makes an amine with one fewer carbon in its skeleton. Hofmann elimination instead concerns a suitable quaternary ammonium species and can produce an alkene plus a tertiary amine. In a supporting ethyltrimethylammonium hydroxide model, the ethyl group supplies a beta hydrogen. Elimination gives ethene, trimethylamine and water. Count five carbons initially: two in the ethyl group and three in methyl groups. The products divide them into two carbons in ethene and three in trimethylamine; no carbon has vanished as a carboxyl derivative. The carbon bearing nitrogen is alpha, and the adjacent ethyl carbon bearing the eliminated hydrogen is beta. A tetramethylammonium ion has no such beta carbon and cannot follow this ordinary alkene forming beta elimination. Where alternative beta sites exist, the familiar Hofmann comparison often favours a less substituted alkene, but substrate geometry and the stated conditions still matter. This supporting distinction is not a general claim that heating any amine releases an alkene or that every named Hofmann process has the same carbon ledger.
points: Ethyltrimethylammonium hydroxide · β-H from ethyl group · Ethene + trimethylamine + H₂O
Carbon count: 2 + 3 = 5 · Product carbons: 2 + 3 · Elimination, not amide rearrangement
Tetramethylammonium · No β carbon for this pathway · No ordinary alkene-forming E2

chapters.title: Strong acid changes aniline nitration directing arguments
chapters.formula: Aniline −NH₂: o/p activation; anilinium −NH₃⁺: deactivating, meta directing
chapters.script: An aromatic directing argument must use the species present in the reaction medium. Neutral aniline has a nitrogen lone pair that can donate toward the ring, favouring ortho and para electrophilic substitution. In a strongly acidic nitration mixture, much of it is converted into anilinium. That nitrogen bears a positive charge and no available lone pair for the same donation, so the anilinium substituent is deactivating and meta directing. Direct nitration is therefore not accurately summarized as clean para substitution of unchanged neutral aniline. Mixtures and other complications can occur; a large meta contribution does not establish a universal pure meta product. Protecting the amino group as an amide before the stated nitration changes basicity and moderates activation, and suitable subsequent hydrolysis can restore the amino group. The usual acetanilide comparison favours a para nitro derivative while allowing an ortho product. Do not confuse adding a nitro group to the ring with oxidizing the existing amino nitrogen into a nitro substituent. Draw the protonated or protected starting species before assigning electron donation, orientation and the final workup product.
points: Neutral ArNH₂ · Lone-pair donation to ring · Ortho / para directing
Strong acid: ArNH₃⁺ · Donation suppressed; ring deactivated · Meta-directing species
Acetanilide protection map · Nitration then stated hydrolysis · Often para-favoured; not universal purity

chapters.title: Aniline binds a Friedel–Crafts Lewis acid
chapters.formula: ArNH₂ → AlCl₃ coordination uses the nitrogen lone pair; usual ring alkylation is unsuitable
chapters.script: An amino substituent activates an aromatic ring in some reactions, but that does not guarantee compatibility with every electrophilic substitution reagent. In the usual aluminium chloride mediated Friedel Crafts comparison, aniline's nitrogen acts as a Lewis base and binds the Lewis acid. The lone pair used in coordination is no longer available in the same way to activate the ring, and the resulting strongly deactivating complex prevents the ordinary clean ring alkylation prediction. Therefore benzene and aniline cannot simply be assigned the same alkyl chloride and aluminium chloride arrow with only a change in directing position. This limitation concerns that reagent system, not universal chemical inertness of aniline. Also distinguish ring acylation from nitrogen acylation: formation of acetanilide makes a new nitrogen carbonyl bond and is not proof that a Friedel Crafts carbon carbon bond formed on the ring. When a question proposes aniline becoming an ethyl substituted aniline through the usual Friedel Crafts conditions, flag the incompatibility before counting ortho and para products. Check Lewis acid binding, substrate activation and the atom actually receiving a new group as three separate decisions.
points: Aniline nitrogen: Lewis base · AlCl₃: Lewis acid · N-lone-pair coordination
Usual Friedel–Crafts system · Complex deactivates aromatic ring · Clean ring alkylation unsuitable
Acetanilide formation · Acyl group bonds to nitrogen · Not ring Friedel–Crafts acylation

chapters.title: Diazonium fluorination uses a different reagent map
chapters.formula: ArN₂⁺BF₄⁻ → ArF + N₂ + BF₃ in the classical Balz–Schiemann map
chapters.script: A diazonium replacement must name the incoming group and the appropriate reaction route. In the classical Balz Schiemann map, an arenediazonium tetrafluoroborate gives an aryl fluoride with nitrogen gas and boron trifluoride on decomposition under the specified reaction conditions. For a benzene derived example, the organic product is fluorobenzene, with the six ring carbons retained. The net atom ledger starts with four fluorines in tetrafluoroborate: one enters the aryl fluoride and three remain with boron in boron trifluoride. Both nitrogens of the diazonium group leave together as one nitrogen molecule. This differs from the familiar copper one chloride or bromide replacement maps; drawing copper fluoride as though all copper assisted replacement reagents were interchangeable is not the intended classical route. Replacing the amino derived diazonium group by fluorine adds no carbon and leaves no nitrogen in the selected organic product. The reaction name describes a controlled chemical transformation, not a guarantee that every substituted ring behaves identically. This chapter supplies reaction and atom accounting, not instructions for isolating or heating a diazonium salt. Keep the counterion, organic substitution and gaseous products distinct.

chapters.title: Diazotization can remove a temporary amino directing group
chapters.formula: ArNH₂ → ArN₂⁺ → ArH using the specified diazotization then H₃PO₂ reduction map
chapters.script: An amino group can help choose where another group enters an aromatic ring and then be removed from the final framework. In the familiar deamination map, a primary aromatic amine is first converted to an arenediazonium species. Reduction with hypophosphorous acid replaces the diazonium group by hydrogen while nitrogen gas is released. Consider a ring labelled with amino at carbon one, methyl at carbon four, and bromines already at carbons two and six. Those bromines are ortho to the amino group in the supplied precursor. Replacing the amino derived diazonium group by hydrogen preserves the ring and methyl carbons. Renumbering the product from its methyl substituent places the bromines at positions three and five, giving three five dibromotoluene. The bromine atoms have not migrated; only the naming reference changed after the directing group was removed. This can achieve a substitution pattern that direct bromination of toluene would not normally favour. The example starts from the specified substituted precursor and does not assume an unqualified bromination gives a single pure product. Follow the original ring labels through replacement before assigning the final product name.

chapters.title: Reductive amination retains the substituent already attached to nitrogen
chapters.formula: CH₃CHO + CH₃NH₂ ⇌ CH₃CH=NCH₃ + H₂O; reduction → CH₃CH₂NHCH₃
chapters.script: The class of an amine product depends on which groups remain attached to nitrogen, not just on whether a carbonyl was reduced. Use a specified reductive amination map starting from acetaldehyde and methylamine. Condensation gives an imine intermediate, meaning a carbon nitrogen double bond compound, with an ethylidene carbon nitrogen double bond and the original methyl group still bonded to nitrogen. The carbonyl oxygen leaves in the water balance rather than remaining in the selected carbon nitrogen double bond intermediate. Reducing the carbon nitrogen double bond then gives ethylmethylamine. Nitrogen is bonded to an ethyl group, a methyl group and one hydrogen, so the product is a secondary amine. The organic inventory is three carbons: two from acetaldehyde and one from methylamine. In formal atom bookkeeping, acetaldehyde plus methylamine plus two reducing hydrogen equivalents gives the three carbon amine plus water. Direct reduction of acetaldehyde alone would instead give ethanol, a different functional group. Actual reductive amination requires suitable control of condensation and reduction, and competing reactions can affect yield. This supporting reaction map identifies connectivity and atom sources rather than prescribing a complete reagent sequence or claiming exclusive conversion.

chapters.title: Supporting extraction: protonation changes the amine distribution ratio
chapters.formula: D=P/(1+10^(pKa(BH⁺)−pH)); forg=D Vorg/(Vaq+D Vorg)
chapters.script: Partition of an amine requires both its acid base equilibrium and its neutral species partition coefficient. In a supplied supporting model, neutral base B distributes between an organic phase and water with coefficient P equal to twenty, defined as organic neutral concentration divided by aqueous neutral concentration. Protonated base remains in water. The conjugate acid has supplied p K a ten, and an external buffer maintains the stated aqueous p H. The ratio of protonated to neutral base in water is ten raised to p K a minus p H. The total organic to aqueous analytical distribution ratio is consequently P divided by one plus that ratio. At p H eight, D is twenty over one hundred one. For one hundred millilitres water and fifty millilitres organic phase, the fraction of total amine in organic solution is ten over one hundred eleven, about nine point zero one percent. At p H ten, D becomes ten and the organic fraction five sixths, about eighty three point three percent. These results assume equilibrium, unchanged phase volumes, no ion transfer into organic solution and no additional association. The supplied p H is maintained rather than calculated from the amine alone.

quiz.question: (CH3)3CNH2 is a:
quiz.explanation: Only one carbon group is bonded directly to nitrogen; carbon branching does not define the amine class.

quiz.question: Reduction of CH3CN gives:
quiz.explanation: The nitrile carbon is retained and becomes the CH2 bonded to NH2, giving a two-carbon amine.

quiz.question: Hofmann rearrangement of CH3CONH2 gives the organic amine:
quiz.explanation: The carbonyl carbon is removed from the organic product, leaving the one-carbon methyl group attached to NH2.

quiz.question: A reliable general aqueous basicity rule is:
options: Solvation and structure must both be considered
quiz.explanation: Electron donation, resonance, crowding and solvent stabilization compete; no single substitution ranking is universal.

quiz.question: The standard carbylamine test is associated with:
quiz.explanation: Primary aliphatic and aromatic amines can give the isocyanide test; secondary and tertiary amines do not.

quiz.question: Azo coupling produces the linkage:
options: N2 gas as the only product

quiz.question: At 25°C with pKw = 14, conjugate-acid pKa = 10 gives base pKb:
quiz.explanation: pKa + pKb = 14 for the conjugate pair under these conditions.

quiz.question: Diazonium replacement by CN on an otherwise unsubstituted six-carbon ring gives how many carbons in the nitrile?
quiz.explanation: The cyano group contributes one additional carbon.

quiz.question: The sulfonamide from a primary amine can dissolve in alkali because it:
quiz.explanation: The retained sulfonamide N-H can be deprotonated under suitable alkaline conditions.

quiz.question: An azo product joining two unsubstituted six-carbon aromatic rings contains:
quiz.explanation: Six plus six carbons gives twelve; the N=N bridge contributes nitrogen and no carbon.

quiz.question: Propanamide under a suitable Hofmann rearrangement gives mainly:
quiz.explanation: The amide carbonyl carbon is lost from the amine skeleton: three starting carbons give two.

quiz.question: Acylation of aniline with an acetyl group on nitrogen gives:
quiz.explanation: The product is an amide, with the nitrogen attached to an acetyl carbonyl group.

quiz.question: The primary-amine sulfonamide in the standard Hinsberg comparison retains:
options: An N–H that can be deprotonated by alkali
quiz.explanation: Its remaining nitrogen hydrogen explains the introductory alkali-solubility distinction.

quiz.question: Aniline → diazonium → nitrile → carboxylic acid gives a final main organic product with:
quiz.explanation: Incoming cyanide adds one carbon to the six-carbon ring, retained on nitrile hydrolysis.

quiz.question: Two bases have pKb 4 and 9 in the same medium. Kb(first)/Kb(second) is:
quiz.explanation: 10^−4 divided by 10^−9 equals 10^5.

quiz.question: At 25 °C in water, pKb(B)=4 gives approximate pKa(BH+) of:
quiz.explanation: Use pKa(BH+) + pKb(B) ≈ 14 for a conjugate pair under the stated conditions.

quiz.question: In a suitable Gabriel synthesis starting with an ethyl fragment, the released target primary amine is:

Every chloride is inert in all chemistry
It already contains an amino group

quiz.explanation: Divide the gas-derived reacting amount by the aliquot solution volume, not by the gas volume.

A change in nitrogen atomic number

quiz.question: In common strong-acid protonation discussions, an amide often preferentially protonates at:
quiz.explanation: Carbonyl oxygen is commonly the preferred amide protonation site; conditions and structure still matter.

quiz.question: A diazonium replacement that releases N2 removes how many nitrogens from the diazonium group?

quiz.question: A simple benzene-derived diazonium fragment couples with a phenol ring. The product carbon count is:

Four carbon bonds and a positive formal charge

quiz.question: Why can tetramethylammonium not give an ordinary alkene by this beta-elimination pathway?

quiz.explanation: All methyl carbons are directly attached to nitrogen; there is no adjacent beta carbon for ordinary E2 alkene formation.

quiz.question: Which species explains a meta-directing contribution during direct aniline nitration in strong acid?

quiz.question: Nitration of protected aniline followed by suitable amide hydrolysis is a map designed to:

Make nitrogen disappear as N2 in every case
Moderate amino-group reactivity and then restore NH2
Convert all anilines into a single universal product
quiz.explanation: Protection changes the electronic and acid-base behaviour; product ratios still depend on substrate and conditions.

quiz.question: Why is the usual alkyl chloride/AlCl3 Friedel–Crafts ring alkylation unsuitable for aniline?
options: AlCl3 must donate a nitrogen atom
Aniline cannot react with any reagent
Nitrogen coordinates the Lewis acid and the ring becomes deactivated
quiz.explanation: Lewis acid binding changes the substrate, invalidating a simple neutral-aniline activation argument.

quiz.question: Acetanilide formation from aniline is primarily:
quiz.explanation: The new acyl group attaches to nitrogen; that is distinct from making a ring carbon–carbon bond.

quiz.question: The classical thermal reaction map for ArN₂⁺BF₄⁻ gives:
quiz.explanation: One fluorine enters the aryl fluoride, three remain with boron, and both diazonium nitrogens leave as N2.

quiz.question: For benzenediazonium tetrafluoroborate in that map, the selected organic product contains:

quiz.question: The specified H₃PO₂ reduction of an arenediazonium group replaces that group by:

quiz.question: A precursor has NH₂ at ring C1, CH₃ at C4 and Br at C2/C6. Removing the amino group through the specified diazonium reduction gives:
quiz.explanation: The original bromines stay at their carbons. Changing the naming reference to methyl makes those positions 3 and 5.
